brief.notification_title: Hot jobs, soft costs: sell the tech bounce, await CPI
brief.market_summary: US stocks finished a rough week with a Friday tech bounce. The S&P 500 closed at 7,376.86 (+0.31% on the day, -2.68% on the week, its worst week since June). The Nasdaq rose 1.09% but lost 3.37% on the week and is in a correction. SMH gained 3.6% after Thursday's 12% drop in the semiconductor index. The Dow fell 0.46% as October's 165K payrolls beat raised the odds of a December hike. Treasuries flattened: the 2Y rose 5bp to 4.51% and the 10Y only 2bp to 4.86%, which is still 37bp lower than a month ago. Brent closed flat at $98.32 but lost about 16% on the week, its biggest weekly drop since 2020. Crypto is drifting near its lows (BTC $75.7k, ETH $2,239) while spot bitcoin ETFs keep losing money.
brief.since_last:
The last brief went out Friday at about 12:27 ET, after payrolls and in the middle of the bounce. Since then:
- The Nasdaq held its gain into the close (+1.09%) and the Dow faded to -237 points (n139). Rate-sensitive defensives lagged: XLP -1.28%, XLU -0.39%. The dollar rose 0.72% and gold fell 0.94%.
- Treasuries: the official curve shows the 2Y up 5bp, the 10Y up 2bp and the 30Y up 1bp. That is a bear flattener, consistent with more Fed hike pricing (n175, n171).
- Iran: Trump said the US carried out "minor strikes" on Iran after missiles hit Qeshm Island near Hormuz (n95). Brent closed flat at $98.32, so it is not clear the strikes are fully priced. This is the main weekend gap risk for Monday's open.
- Crypto ETFs: spot bitcoin ETFs lost $412M on Nov 6 (IBIT -$403M) and ether ETFs lost $93.2M, the second heavy day in a row. Bitcoin ETFs had their largest weekly outflow since June (n40). One source reports +$252.5M of inflows instead; it doesn't match the others and I'm ignoring it.
- Berkshire more than doubled Q3 buybacks while earnings fell (n4).
- Late Friday data: consumer credit was $27.84B vs $13.40B expected. CFTC positioning shows speculators trimmed their Nasdaq net longs to 42.9K from 48.8K and added to crude net longs (80.3K from 74.3K).
- Data caveats: the economic calendar's timestamps look shifted by a day, so payrolls show as 11-07. The calendar also lists "no scheduled events" next week, which the research contradicts (CPI is Tuesday). I've used the research for next week's schedule.

economic_data.takeaway: It beat even the highest Bloomberg forecast (131K). This is the main reason December hike odds rose (n171, n96). Front-end yields rose and the dollar firmed (+0.72%).
The headline rate fell, but U6 rose 0.3pt to 7.9%. There is more part-time and marginal slack under the surface than the headline shows. The Fed will watch the headline; I'm noting the divergence.
Wages were a touch hot on the month but cooled year on year. With CPI running near 3.7–3.9%, real wages are still negative (n160). That supports hiking but doesn't point to a wage-price spiral.

This is the most underrated release of the week. Falling labor costs per unit of output are disinflationary for margins and prices, and they support the long end of the Treasury curve even if the Fed hikes.
Sentiment improved and inflation expectations fell. That helps the Fed's credibility and caps long-end inflation premium, which supports buying IEF on a back-up in yields.
Layoffs remain low. Continuing claims are creeping up, so hiring is slow even though firing is rare.
Strong borrowing adds to the picture of a resilient economy and gives the Fed room to hike. It's a marginal negative for bonds.

This is the key event of the week. A 0.2% core print with energy driving the headline lets the long end rally and could fill nothing on my IEF limits. Core at 0.4% or more would likely push the 10Y toward 4.95–5.05%, where my IEF bids sit, and would hit tech again.
It lands on the day all three idea orders expire, so it's the last input before I reassess them.

Supply right after a hot jobs report usually needs a price concession. Sources disagree on the 10Y size ($39B vs $42B), so check Treasury's announcement. Weak tails would push yields toward my IEF limit levels.

sections.summary: Friday was a reflex bounce in chips after Thursday's capitulation-type day. The week still damaged the AI leadership: XLK -8.2%, SMH -11.2%, Nasdaq in a correction. Money is rotating into health care, financials and consumer discretionary, which are up 5–10% over the month. The hot jobs report weighed on the Dow and defensives, and the coming week of CPI, AMAT and CSCO will decide whether the bounce holds.

SMH +3.62% Friday after the semiconductor index fell 12% Thursday, its worst day since March 2020. XLK closed at 164.74, still below the $168–170 trim limits.

sections.summary: The jobs beat moved the front end, not the long end. The 2Y rose 5bp to 4.51% while the 10Y rose 2bp to 4.86% and the 30Y 1bp to 5.26%, a bear flattener that prices more Fed hikes and less long-run inflation. Credit barely moved despite the equity rout: HYG -0.26% and LQD +0.25% on the week. Next week brings ~$125B of refunding supply around Tuesday's CPI.
key_points: Official curve 11/06: 3M 4.19%, 2Y 4.51%, 10Y 4.86%, 30Y 5.26%; 2s10s +35bp. The 10Y is still -37bp over the month.
Fed tone is hawkish: policymakers are considering a hike (n171), Daly warns of more (n112), Zandi sees a 'very high probability' in December (n96). Williams wants more inflation data first (n173).
Disinflation evidence: unit labor costs -0.7%, Michigan 1Y inflation expectations 4.3% from 4.7%.

Headlines quoting a 2Y at 4.46% (-12bp) and a 19bp 10Y drop (n117, n93) appear to describe Thursday or intraday moves; I'm using the Treasury par curve. Foreign holdings of Treasuries are declining (n169), a structural support for term premium.

Friday's $96.65–100.92 range shows the two-way risk: tanker attacks in Hormuz and Trump's 'minor strikes' on Iran (n95) against reports of an Iranian nuclear proposal through Qatar. The weekend strike news hit a market that closed flat, so Monday's open is the first real test.

brief.instructor_take: Here's how I read the week. AI-capex fears broke tech on Thursday, a political shock hit two of the market's favourite themes (data centers and the war premium in oil), and on Friday a hot jobs report put a December hike back on the table. The crowd will focus on payrolls of 165K against 65K expected. I'd focus on what came with it: unit labor costs fell 0.7%, productivity rose 3.6%, Michigan 1-year inflation expectations fell to 4.3%, and U6 rose to 7.9%. That's an economy that is creating jobs without creating cost pressure. The Fed can hike once or twice, but the long end shouldn't run away, and Friday's bear flattener says the bond market agrees. For stocks, that mix is worst for long-duration tech, which is already fighting Anthropic IPO supply and a backlash against data centers. It is better for health care and the consumer, where earnings are actually coming through (Humana, Moderna, Airbnb). So I'm using bounces in tech to cut risk and waiting for CPI and the auctions to give me better bond yields. I'm keeping dry powder in SGOV, where 3-month bills pay about 4.2% and will reset higher if the Fed hikes. The weekend wildcard is Iran: US strikes came after a week that removed much of oil's war premium, so a Monday gap higher in Brent is plausible. I'm not chasing BNO, but an oil spike would hurt both my IEF bids and the equity bounce. Crypto has no edge for me while ETFs are bleeding. My view would change if CPI core prints 0.2% and AMAT guides up, which together would mean Thursday was a flush rather than the start of a breakdown.

top_ideas.title: Trim tech overweight into the bounce before CPI/AMAT
top_ideas.one_liner: Sell 1/3 of tech overweight at $166.50/$169; backstop $160
top_ideas.thesis: Friday's +1.45% in XLK and +3.6% in SMH look like a reflex bounce after the semiconductor index's worst day since March 2020. The outlook for tech is worse than for other sectors: December hike odds are rising, data-center guidance is getting cut, and an Anthropic IPO could pull capital out of existing AI holdings. Use strength to cut position size before CPI on Tuesday and AMAT on Thursday.
top_ideas.reasoning: I treat a bounce the day after a capitulation-type drop as a chance to sell risk I don't want, not as information about direction. The case against tech has three legs. A 165K payrolls beat makes a December hike likely, which compresses long-duration growth valuations. Atlassian's data-center guide-down and the midterm backlash against data centers (n53) attack the AI-capex story at its source. A $1–1.3T Anthropic listing (n42) would pull money out of existing AI holdings. XLK is down 16.7% in a month, but in a sector shedding leadership a 'cheap' price can keep getting cheaper. I'm lowering the first tranche to $166.50 because Friday closed at 164.74 and I want half of this done before two binary events. Trim SMH instead if that's where your overweight sits. I'd be wrong if XLK closes above $177, which would make Thursday a one-day flush, and a strong AMAT guide is the most likely trigger for that. What a less experienced investor misses: this is about position size, not calling the bottom, which is why I'm selling only a third.

risks: The short-covering rally extends: put/call hit 1.2, speculators are net short S&P, and strategists are urging dip-buying (n44)

Limits don't fill and you hold the full overweight into a further drop (the $160 backstop handles this)
top_ideas.entry: Replace the $168–170 orders with GTC limit sells: half of the one-third at $166.50, half at $169 on XLK (or matching QQQ/SMH bounce levels), good through Fri 13 Nov. Backstop: if XLK closes below $160 before the limits fill, sell the unfilled part at the next close. Put proceeds in SGOV.
top_ideas.invalidation: XLK closes above $177. Stop trimming and reassess.
top_ideas.sizing: One-third of your tech/AI overweight only. Leave core index holdings alone.

top_ideas.title: Buy 7–10Y Treasuries on a CPI/auction back-up
top_ideas.thesis: The Fed is hiking into falling unit labor costs and easing inflation expectations, and the curve is flattening. That combination tends to cap the long end. Don't pay 4.86% into CPI and ~$125B of refunding supply; let auction concessions bring the 10Y to 4.95–5.05%.
top_ideas.reasoning: Friday's curve is the evidence. The 2Y rose 5bp and the 10Y only 2bp on a blowout jobs number, a bear flattener. It means the market reads hikes now as less inflation later. The details back that up: unit labor costs -0.7% against +0.3% expected, productivity +3.6%, Michigan 1Y expectations at 4.3% from 4.7%. But timing matters. CPI is expected at 3.9% y/y on Tuesday, and the 3Y, 10Y and 30Y auctions usually need a price concession, especially after a hot report. I'd rather name my price than chase. My limit levels assume roughly 7 years of duration: about $91.20 at a 4.95% 10Y and $90.60 at 5.05%. I prefer IEF to TLT because it captures most of the rally with less exposure to term premium and falling foreign demand (n169). I'm wrong if the 10Y closes above 5.20%, or if CPI and Fed speakers point to a string of hikes rather than one or two.

top_ideas.entry: GTC limit buy for half at about $91.20 and half at about $90.60, good through Fri 13 Nov. Fund from SGOV. Cancel if the 10Y trades below 4.75% before filling, because the opportunity will have passed.

top_ideas.title: Health care: finish the add only at $184 or lower
top_ideas.one_liner: Second half of XLV at ≤$184; Humana and Moderna beats back it
top_ideas.thesis: Health care is where earnings are holding up during a hiking cycle with AI doubts: Humana beat by a wide margin and Moderna raised guidance. After a 9.9% month I won't chase, though. Finish the position only on a dip to $184 or lower.
top_ideas.reasoning: Rotation matters only when earnings back it, and this week they did. Humana printed $3.24 against an expected loss of $1.03, and Moderna raised 2026 revenue-growth guidance to 15–25%. Those results came while XLK lost 16.7% in a month, which tells me money is moving toward earnings that don't depend on cheap capital or data-center spending. I prefer XLV to staples: XLP fell 1.28% Friday and has less earnings growth to offer when rates are rising. The $181–182 order almost certainly expired unfilled, since XLV closed at 184.80. That's fine, because the first half is already working. The discipline is price. Investors often drop their limits once a trade 'works', and that's how they buy the top of a rotation. I'll drop the idea on a close below $176 or a guidance cut from Humana, Cigna or Novo. I'd also pause if a strong CPI-plus-AMAT combination triggers a sharp rotation back into tech.

risks: XLV is extended (+9.9% in 1M) and could give back gains if tech rebounds

top_ideas.invalidation: XLV closes below $176, or Humana, Cigna or Novo cuts forward guidance.
top_ideas.sizing: Second half of a 3–4% total position, so about 1.5–2% added.

lesson.explanation: A bear flattener is when yields rise across the curve but short-dated yields rise more than long-dated ones, so the curve gets flatter. It usually means the market expects the central bank to tighten soon. Because it also expects that tightening to contain inflation later, it doesn't demand much more yield on long bonds. That's why a flattener can mark a good time to add duration, while a bear steepener (long yields leading the rise) is the dangerous one for bond holders.
lesson.todays_example: After the 165K payrolls beat on Friday, the 2Y rose 5bp to 4.51% while the 10Y rose only 2bp to 4.86% and the 30Y 1bp to 5.26%. The market priced a December hike without pricing an inflation problem, helped by unit labor costs of -0.7% and lower Michigan inflation expectations. That's the basis for bidding IEF on a back-up instead of avoiding duration.
